I know this topic is already very widely discussed here, but its also true that each discussion brings some new understanding to the table.

I want to know that for a solo freelancer who wants to give away some of his code (in order to gain community recognition and/or better career prospects), what should be the ideal way of licensing such code?

The code in question is a PHP DataViz app similar to tableau but light-weight and based on FOSS web-components like bootstrap, jquery, jquery-ui and jqplot.
Is a Copyleft (GPL/LGPL) or Open-Source (MIT/Apache/BSD) license the right way to license their software for a solo developer/freelancer?

It really depends on what you want and how much you're willing to fight over it. If someone takes your code and uses it in their proprietary software, are you willing to sue over it? Are you willing to hand over control to some other group who might sue over it? Are you going to bitch about it but let them do it? Are you just going to ask them to credit you? Choose a license that represents both what you want and what you're actually going to be willing and able to enforce. There isn't one simple answer for everyone.

For me personally the real question is: GPLv2 or BSD? I don't think the other options are different enough to merit consideration and these 2 are arguably the most well known of the bunch.

In the end it is a question of preference: do you want people to give back to the project? If so GPL. If it's something small you don't expect to be credited for or enhanced by others then BSD.

Ideally we should always use BSD but history has shown that large companies can and will use your work for profit despite licensing. If you don't mind, BSD is great but if you want at least to be credited or have them contribute back their work as open source then GPLv2.

And for fuck's sake stay away from GPLv3!
